Get a business energy contract

Types of business energy contracts you can get, and how to set one up.

Contents
How business sizes affect energy contracts
Types of business contracts
Get help to arrange your contract

If you’re starting a new business, moving premises or changing energy suppliers, you’ll need to set up a business energy contract. The terms, pricing and regulations differ from standard home energy contracts.

Find out more about what to do when moving premises or switching business contracts.

The type of contract you can get usually depends on the size of your business, and how much energy you use. Before you agree to a contract, it’s important to know:

what type of contract it is
how long the term is
if there are any fees involved, for example those agreed in special clauses in your contract
what protections you have
if any broker fees or commissions are included in the price

It’s also important to know what happens at the end of your contract, for example if it will automatically renew, or if you will move to out-of-contract or deemed rates.

If you run your business from home

If you work from home you are probably on a domestic energy contract. Check with your energy supplier to make sure.

How business sizes affect energy contracts

The type of contract you need if you run a business will depend on the:

number of people you employ
income your business makes over a year
amount of electricity or gas your business uses a year

Different sizes of businesses get different protections.

Microbusinesses

To qualify as a microbusiness, you must have fewer than 10 employees and an annual turnover or balance sheet total of no more than £2 million.

You can also qualify if you use up to 100,000 kWh per year (electricity) or up to 293,000 kWh per year (gas).

If you are a microbusiness, you have extra protections when arranging or renewing an energy contract. Your energy supplier must:

provide clear information about your contract
limit termination notice periods to 30 days (evergreen contracts only)
acknowledge requests to end a contract within 5 working days (evergreen contracts only)
provide information about renewal prices before your contract ends

Microbusinesses and small businesses can get support with their energy contracts from Citizens Advice. They can also get help with unresolved supplier complaints from the Energy Ombudsman.

Small businesses

To qualify as a small business, you must have 11 to 50 employees and an annual turnover of up to £6.5 million or balance sheet total of no more than £5 million.

You can also qualify if you use up to 200,000 kWh per year (electricity) or up to 500,000 kWh per year (gas).

Large businesses

To qualify as a large business, you must have 50 or more employees and an annual turnover of more than £6.5 million or balance sheet total of more than £5 million.

You can also qualify if you use more than 200,000 kWh per year (electricity) or more than 500,000 kWh per year (gas).

Some suppliers may use either your business size or your annual energy consumption when deciding which contract or protections apply.

Types of business contracts

There are a number of different types of business energy contracts. Energy suppliers may not offer all of them.

Fixed-rate contracts

Fixed rate contracts fix the price of unit rates and standing charges for the length of the contract. This means the cost per kWh remains the same no matter what happens to wholesale market prices.

Variable-rate contracts

With a variable-rate contract, the price you pay for energy can increase or decrease during the contract period. This may be because your prices change when the wholesale market prices change.

Deemed-rate contracts

You will be put on a deemed contract automatically when you move into a new premises without arranging a formal contract. Deemed rates are usually higher than negotiated contract rates.

You will also be put on a deemed rate if your energy supplier goes out of business.

Out of contract rates

Some suppliers move you onto out-of-contract rates if your fixed-term contract ends without you agreeing to a new deal. Like deemed rate contracts, these rates are usually more expensive than fixed-term contracts.

Rollover or evergreen contracts

Some contracts automatically renew at the end of a fixed term contract if you have not made a new arrangement, or switched to a new supplier. The new arrangement will be for a fixed term (usually 12 months), and may be on a higher rate.

Flexible contracts

Flexible contracts (sometimes called structured contracts) are suitable for large businesses that use a lot of energy. Rather than locking into a fixed price, they allow companies to buy energy in smaller portions when market conditions are better.

Get help to arrange your contract

You can arrange your business contract yourself, or you can use an energy broker, consultant or a price comparison service (also known as third-party intermediaries).

Using a price comparison service

Price comparison websites help you compare business gas and electricity contracts from different suppliers. Check which suppliers are included in the comparison, and whether the website compares the whole market or only a selection of suppliers. You should also check whether the website receives commission from energy suppliers or other sources.

Using an energy broker

Energy brokers can help you find a suitable contract for your business, and then negotiate with your chosen supplier. This can save you time and resources.

Brokers charge you for their services. Some charge an upfront fee, but most are paid a commission by the energy supplier you choose. If your broker is paid by an energy supplier, they must be a member of an approved redress scheme.

Before using one, check which scheme they belong to:

Energy Ombudsman broker register
Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA) accredited member list

Because there is no cooling-off period after you agree to your contract, it’s important you make sure you use a trustworthy broker.

Switch your business energy supplier

When and how to switch your business energy contract, including when you are moving to new premises.

Contents
When to switch energy supplier
How to switch business energy supplier
Moving to new business premises

Before deciding to switch your business energy supplier, read the terms and conditions of your existing contract to find out:

when you can switch
how much notice you should give your supplier
if you will need to pay an exit fee

If you work from home you will have a different type of energy contract. Read how to switch your home energy supplier.

When to switch energy supplier

When you can switch depends on the type of contract you agreed with your supplier. Find out more about the different types of contract available.

Read what to do if your energy supplier goes out of business.

Fixed-rate contracts

Most suppliers will not let you switch before the end of your contract unless you have already agreed a termination clause or pay an exit fee.

Fixed-rate contracts include a ‘switching window’, a set period of time for you to renew with your supplier or tell them you intend to leave. This window opens a few months before the end of your contract.

You can sometimes switch during this window without paying a fee. Check your contract or talk to your supplier or energy broker for more information.

Variable-rate contracts

If you have not agreed a fixed-rate contract or if your contract has expired, you may be on:

a rolling or ‘evergreen’ contract
out-of-contract rates
a deemed-rate contract

With a variable-rate contract, you can switch to a new supplier at any time.

How to switch business energy supplier

You should compare energy prices and contract offers to find the one that is right for you. The best option may be with your current supplier.

You can get information on what is available directly from suppliers or by using an intermediary like a price comparison website or energy broker.

Find out more about using an intermediary to help you get an energy contract.

You will need to give your new supplier some information before signing your contract, including your annual consumption and details of your meter.

Your existing supplier may object to your switch, for example if you owe them money. If this happens, get in touch with them as soon as possible to find out what the issue is and how to resolve it.

Moving to new business premises

You may want to switch to a new supplier or business energy contract for your new premises. You should check if you can do this before you move, and follow the usual switching process.

You are responsible for any energy you use in the period before your new contract starts. If you use energy in this period, your supplier could put you onto a deemed-rate contract.

Read how the change of tenancy process works for businesses.

sources.title: Ofgem confirms greater protection for businesses | Ofgem
sources.extracted_content:
Ofgem confirms greater protection for businesses
Publication type:
Press release
Publication date:
5 April 2024
Topic: Gas supply
Print this page
Share the page
Share on Facebook
Share on X
Share on LinkedIn

Businesses will get fairer treatment, more support resolving disputes and greater transparency on broker fees under new rules announced by Ofgem today.

The changes will apply to the non-domestic energy sector, which includes businesses, public services like sports centres and village halls, utilities, charities and more. The new rules will make sure energy suppliers improve customer service, open doors to alternative dispute resolution schemes and clearly set out costs for businesses, including fees paid for third party services, like energy brokers.

Under the changes, Ofgem will from 1 July 2024:

Expand the Standards of Conduct to apply to all businesses of any size, rather than just Micro Business consumers. This will give Ofgem powers to take action against suppliers that do not treat non-domestic customers fairly.
Introduce a new supply licence rule for non-domestic suppliers which requires them to signpost Micro Business consumers to Citizens Advice and Citizens Advice Scotland, who can offer support and advice when they have an issue. This will also apply to Small Business consumers from December 2024, subject to the new definition entering legislation.

Further changes, that Ofgem expects to be in place by the end of the year, include:

Expanding the requirement for a contract’s principal terms to clearly display any broker fees from Micro Business consumers to all non-domestic customers. This will apply to contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024 and suppliers must make this information available upon request.

From December 2024, in line with the government’s proposed new Small Business consumer definition entering legislation, Ofgem will also:

Update the Complaints Handling Standards to ensure suppliers put in place suitable complaints processes for Small Business consumers and point them to the Energy Ombudsman when a customer does not feel the issue has been resolved.
Implement a requirement for suppliers to only work with Third-party Intermediaries (TPIs), often referred to as brokers, that are members of a redress scheme when securing Small Business contracts. This will provide reassurance to business customers that they are able to access dispute resolution schemes and get a fair and suitable outcome.

Tim Jarvis, Ofgem’s Director General for Markets, said:

"Too many businesses have experienced issues with some energy suppliers, from difficulty getting the right contracts, unexplained price hikes, and poor customer service.

“We’ve worked hard to understand the breadth of issues and where the powers we have to tackle them can be improved. These new rules will help ensure businesses get the service they deserve.

“We’ll be speaking to businesses of all sizes as these rules come into force throughout this year to make sure they are being followed by suppliers. We’ll also continue to work with government, industry, and consumer groups to see what else can be done to support non-domestic consumers.”

Ofgem’s new rules come as the government confirms plans to expand its definition of Small Businesses, meaning businesses with less than 50 employees and a certain turnover or using a certain amount of energy can take complaints about their energy supplier to the Energy Ombudsman.

Under new Ofgem rules, Small Businesses will also be able to resolve disputes about third parties like energy brokers with redress scheme providers, such as the Energy Ombudsman and the Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA). This was previously only available for Micro Business consumers so the change will give more businesses access to independent support with complaints.

The changes being brought in by Ofgem to help businesses result from concerns shared last year about problems including poor customer service and complaint handling from those in the non-domestic energy market. This prompted a joint deep dive to learn more about these issues with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), the full results of which have now been published.

More than half of those taking part in the research (58%) said they were concerned about the impact of energy prices on their business, with 42% reporting they were very concerned. And almost two thirds (60%) of businesses were satisfied with the overall service they had received from their supplier, with 13% saying that they were dissatisfied.

The main reasons consumers said they were dissatisfied included the service being too expensive, poor customer service, and poor communication from their supplier.

NOTES TO EDITORS
A Micro Business consumer uses less than 100,000 kWh of electricity a year; uses less than 293,000 kWh of gas a year; or has fewer than 10 employees (or their full-time equivalent) and an annual turnover total not exceeding 2 million Euros (equivalent to £1.716m according on 22 March 2024).
Today’s announcement aligns with the new Government definition of Small Business and support from the Energy Ombudsman to cover businesses with fewer than 50 employees and an annual turnover of £6.5 million or a balance sheet total of £5 million; or an annual electricity consumption level of 200,000kWh; or an annual gas consumption level of 500,000 kWh.
We are currently aware of two redress schemes in operation which can provide support in resolving consumers' disputes with an energy broker:
The Energy Ombudsman
The Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA)
The new changes being introduced follow from a Call for Input on the Non-Domestic Gas and Electricity Market and a Non-Domestic Market Review Findings and Policy Consultation. The statutory consultation on the proposals ended earlier this year.
We recently published a report of findings from research conducted with non-domestic energy customers. This research was commissioned by Ofgem and DESNZ to build on existing evidence about non-domestic consumers’ experiences of the energy market.

Can my business get help from Energy Ombudsman?
Published Aug 12, 2025

Energy Ombudsman is currently able to offer free independent dispute resolution services to small businesses and microbusinesses. This means that we can help as much as 99% of businesses in Great Britain.

Energy Ombudsman is currently able to offer free independent dispute resolution services to small businesses and microbusinesses. This means that we can help as much as 99% of businesses in Great Britain.

This change ensures that small businesses and microbusinesses have access to a free, impartial, and independent service to help resolve disputes with their Energy Suppliers, Energy Brokers, Heat Networks, Network Operators, Flexibility Service Providers, and Green Deal.

What is classed as a small business?

If your business meets certain criteria, it may be classed by energy suppliers and brokers as a small business. According to Ofgem's definition, a small business energy consumer must meet the following conditions:

The small business has fewer than 50 employees or their full-time equivalent, AND an annual turnover of at most £6.5 million or a balance sheet total of £5.0 million
OR an annual electricity consumption of not more than 200,000 kWh
OR an annual gas consumption of not more than 500,000 kWh

You might be a small business for one type of energy usage and not the other - it depends on the amount you use. This may mean you have different quotes from your supplier or broker for your gas and electricity.

We’re able to accept disputes providing they meet our Terms of Reference. You‘ll need to follow your supplier or energy broker’s complaints processes first. Then after 8 weeks, or if a deadlock letter has been issued to you, we may be able to help with your dispute.

What is classed as a microbusiness?

Ofgem defines a microbusiness energy consumer when:

The business has fewer than 10 employees (or their full-time equivalent) AND your yearly turnover or yearly balance sheet, is not more than £2 million
OR an annual electricity consumption of not more than 100,000 kWh
OR an annual gas consumption of not more than 293,000 kWh

We’re able to accept disputes providing they meet our Terms of Reference. You‘ll need to follow your supplier or energy broker’s complaints processes first. Then after 8 weeks, or if a deadlock letter has been issued to you, we may be able to help with your dispute.

How can we help your business?

If you’re satisfied that your business is a small business or microbusiness, we may be able to look into any disputes you have with your energy supplier or broker. You’ll have to follow their complaints process first and give them 8 weeks to provide a resolution. If they’re unable to resolve your complaint in 8 weeks, or offer you a deadlock letter or "final response" before then, we may be able to offer dispute resolution.

FAQs
How much energy does a small business use?
expand_more

A small business is one that has an annual electricity consumption of not more than 200,000 kWh OR an annual gas consumption of not more than 500,000 kWh OR the small business has fewer than 50 employees or their full-time equivalent, AND an annual turnover of at most £6.5 million or a balance sheet total of £5.0 million.

thumb_up thumb_down Share
Can Energy Ombudsman support microbusinesses?
expand_more

Yes, Energy Ombudsman is able to support microbusinesses. A microbusiness is a business that uses less than 100,000 kWh of electricity per year, less than 293,000 kWh of gas per year, or has fewer than 10 employees AND your yearly turnover or yearly balance sheet, is not more than £2 million.

sources.title: Managing business energy costs in an uncertain market | Ofgem
sources.extracted_content:
Managing business energy costs in an uncertain market
Jemma Baker
Deputy Director - Future Retail Markets - Consumer Protection and Competition
Publication type:
Blog
Publication date:
31 March 2026
Topic: Non-domestic energy supply
Subtopic: Third party intermediaries
Print this page
Share the page
Share on Facebook
Share on X
Share on LinkedIn

The price you pay for energy for your business can vary across suppliers and the type and size of your business, but covers a range of costs including the wholesale energy cost (the cost to buy energy), network costs (the infrastructure to transport energy), and environmental costs (government decarbonisation schemes). Typically, wholesale costs can be about 40% of your electricity bill and about 60% of your gas bill, but exact percentages will vary.

In April, network costs are increasing to upgrade energy infrastructure. Wholesale energy costs are volatile and will continue to be affected by the situation in the Middle East.

Our understanding is that the majority of businesses are not currently exposed to immediate price increases as contract lengths are starting to return to 3 to 5 years in length. Based on current evidence, we expect less than 10% of businesses to recontract in March and April, with a further 10-12% currently on deemed contracts, and a further 10% likely to recontract in May to July.

However, if your fixed price contract is coming to an end, you will need to negotiate a new contract with your supplier.

Talk to your supplier about your contract options

If your current contract is coming to an end, talk to your supplier about what options are available.  If you have an energy broker, they can do this for you.

Consider your options

Ask suppliers what contracts are available and consider both short and long-term options. It may be better for you to temporarily stay on deemed or out of contract rates if the current longer-term contract offers are high.

Things to be aware of

When thinking about your contract options, you should be aware that:

suppliers may require security deposits because of greater risks of businesses defaulting on payment
energy suppliers are not obliged to offer businesses a contract and offers may be harder to find
you shouldn’t feel pressured into signing a contract and there is no cooling off period, so check the terms and fees beforehand
if you discuss a contract over the phone, you should ask for it in writing before agreeing it
you can avoid fraudsters by verifying unexpected calls. If in doubt about the caller, stop and check their details
Keep in contact with your supplier

Your supplier must treat you fairly and bill you accurately based on your meter readings. To ensure you are only paying for what you use, submit regular meter readings or get a smart meter. It is also important you keep your contact details up to date so that you receive your bills.

If you are having problems managing your bill, you should talk to your supplier or your energy broker. Your supplier can also offer you advice on reducing your bill.

Get help if your business cannot afford its energy bills.

Ways to get help

Managing energy for your business is just one of many competing demands. There is support available to help you. You can contact:

reputable energy brokers who can talk to suppliers for you
trade bodies, consumer groups and charities who can offer detailed advice and support
the Energy Ombudsman for small businesses, who can help if you get into a dispute with your supplier and you cannot resolve your complaint; if your dispute is with your energy broker, they will provide details of their redress scheme provider to contact

You could be eligible for financial assistance or schemes that help you reduce energy costs:

Find business energy efficiency grants and schemes.

Get advice on business recontracting.

Find out more about the costs included in your bills.

Climate Change Levy

Climate Change Levy is paid at either, or both the:

main levy rate

As a business energy supplier you’re responsible for charging the correct levy to your customers.

The rates do not apply to taxable commodities supplied to domestic consumers and charities for non-business use.

Find business energy efficiency grants and schemes

This guide will help you find small business energy grants, schemes and advice to lower your carbon emissions and get more efficient with your commercial energy use. This can help you save money and become more environmentally friendly.

Energy efficiency advice

The National Energy Foundation website offers free, independent advice on efficient energy usage and installing sources of renewable energy.

The Energy Savings Trust website lists example case studies, energy efficiency resources and runs events to help businesses make informed choices, including supply chain advice.

The Smallbusiness.co.uk website also provides a range of online energy efficiency news for small business owners, including start-ups.

You can check GOV.UK’s Energy Technology List if you are planning new plant equipment. It covers independently verified energy-efficient products such as boilers, lighting, air conditioning and refrigeration equipment.

Then look at business-finance support schemes offered by suppliers and the government that may be able to pay for improvements. Some specialist agencies or charities may run funding and support schemes too. Ask around for information in your business networks.

Government business energy schemes, loans and grants

Many government schemes offer loans, grants or subsidised energy-saving measures to support small businesses with reducing their impact on the environment. These normally help with:

energy efficiency measures – such as revising production processes
the upfront costs of investing in energy-efficient equipment
waste management and reduction initiatives
sustainable development initiatives.

Start by searching the GOV.UK business finance and support finder.

Ask your local council if they provide energy efficiency funding or sustainable business growth grants. You will normally need to submit a business case to apply. Some initiatives may also be eligible for business innovation funding.

See if you can get paid to generate your own renewable power and heat through the national Smart Export Guarantee scheme.

The government is also proposing two new energy efficiency schemes from 2022 to replace the current domestic and non-domestic renewable heat incentives.

Clean Heat Grant: upfront capital funding for households or businesses that integrate green heating technologies such as heat pumps and in certain circumstances biomass.
Green Gas Support Scheme: funding support for biomethane injection to increase the amount of green gas in the national grid.

Ofgem is the intended schemes administrator. We will publish more information as the Government progresses with its proposals. Visit our Environmental and Social schemes area to find out more.

Business grants and services from energy suppliers

Energy companies may offer small business energy-efficiency schemes or grants.

Eligibility criteria and availability will vary, depending on things like:

the size of your business
your location
your business sector.

Contact your supplier to find out what they offer.

Other business energy grants and support services

Try free grants search services, like Grants Online.

WRAP may offer grants and investments supporting business waste reduction costs.

Further help

Citizens Advice offers free, independent advice about business energy contracts and your rights.

Call 0808 223 1133 or use their online webchat.
For textphone, dial 18001 followed by the helpline number.
Someone at their Extra Help Unit could take on your case if you are having difficulties with a supplier and are in a vulnerable situation.

You can also contact the government’s free Business Support Helplines.

Related content
Getting help if your business cannot afford its energy bills

Call your supplier to agree a payment plan and get emergency help. Contact Citizens Advice for more support: 0808 223 1133.

Environmental and social schemes
Ofgem's role

Ofgem administers renewable energy and social schemes on behalf of the government. Our administration of the energy and social programmes aligns with our activities as a regulator and these programmes focus on renewable heat, renewable electricity, energy efficiency and fuel poverty.

We work with energy companies, consumer groups and other stakeholders, including the UK’s elected representatives and other delivery partners across government, to make sure policy targets are met in an economical and consumer conscious way.

Supplier obligations

Licenced electricity suppliers in Great Britain are obligated under many of these environmental and social schemes. The nature and level of obligations depend on a supplier’s:

licence types (gas or electricity)
supply volumes
domestic supply customer count

To help suppliers meet these obligations, we have briefly outlined the purpose and requirements for each environmental and social scheme along with links to further information in our guide: Supplier obligations: environmental and social schemes.

Supplier Performance Report

The Supplier Performance Report documents incidents where energy suppliers have not complied with their obligations under the environmental, energy efficiency and social programmes we administer on behalf of the government.

Counter fraud

Our performance

Our data shows details of our performance against our 3 key indicators:

how quickly we respond to stakeholders.
how long payments and processing take.
the availability of our IT systems for scheme participants
Scheme performance indicators

Every year we commit to upholding specific service levels for the GB Domestic and Non-Domestic RHI, Feed-In-Tariffs, Renewables Obligation, Energy Company Obligation and Warm Home Discount schemes. These are documented within the key performance indicators section of the Ofgem Forward Work Programme. Meeting or exceeding these indicators is important to us as we want to provide the best possible service to our customers.

Out-of-contract rates apply if a fixed term ends without a new deal and are usually more expensive than fixed-term contracts. Rollover/evergreen contracts renew automatically; the new arrangement is usually for 12 months and may be at a higher rate. Flexible (structured) contracts suit large, high-use businesses and let them buy energy in smaller portions when market conditions are better, instead of locking in one fixed price.
findings.limitations: The page has no date. It is a general overview with no typical unit-rate or standing-charge figures. It does not explain pass-through of non-commodity charges. It describes flexible contracts only as 'suitable for large businesses'.

findings.claim: Terms to check before agreeing a contract: contract type, term length, fees (including special clauses), protections, broker fees or commission, and what happens at the end of the contract (auto-renewal, or a move to out-of-contract or deemed rates). Microbusinesses get extra protections.
findings.evidence: Ofgem lists these points to know before agreeing to a contract. Microbusiness is defined as fewer than 10 employees and turnover or balance sheet of no more than £2 million, or use of up to 100,000 kWh a year of electricity. Suppliers must give clear contract information and information on renewal prices before the contract ends. For evergreen contracts only, they must limit termination notice periods to 30 days and acknowledge requests to end a contract within 5 working days. There is no cooling-off period after agreeing a contract. Brokers are usually paid commission by the supplier, and this may be included in the price.
findings.limitations: The protections listed are for microbusinesses. Small and large businesses get different protections that the page doesn't detail. The page doesn't cover price-variation clauses specifically.

findings.claim: Termination and switching rights depend on contract type. Fixed-rate contracts usually carry exit fees for leaving early and have a pre-expiry 'switching window'. Variable, evergreen, out-of-contract and deemed contracts can be left at any time.
findings.evidence: Ofgem says most suppliers will not let you switch before the end of a fixed contract unless you have agreed a termination clause or pay an exit fee. Fixed-rate contracts include a 'switching window' that opens a few months before the end, during which you can sometimes switch without a fee. For variable-rate arrangements (rolling/evergreen, out-of-contract, deemed) "you can switch to a new supplier at any time". Customers should read their terms to check when they can switch, how much notice to give, and whether an exit fee applies. A business using energy in new premises before a contract starts could be put on a deemed-rate contract.
findings.limitations: The page has no date. It gives no exit-fee amounts or notice-period lengths beyond what S1 states. The statement that variable-rate arrangements can be switched at any time is Ofgem's general wording, so individual supplier terms should still be checked.

findings.claim: Ofgem defines microbusiness and small business consumers, and these definitions determine which protections apply. Microbusinesses get extra protections at contract renewal and end of contract.
findings.evidence: S1 (Ofgem): a microbusiness has fewer than 10 employees and turnover or balance sheet of no more than £2 million, or uses up to 100,000 kWh a year of electricity (293,000 kWh gas). Suppliers must give clear contract information and renewal-price information before the contract ends. For evergreen contracts only, they must limit termination notice to 30 days and acknowledge termination requests within 5 working days. A small business has 11 to 50 employees and turnover up to £6.5 million or balance sheet up to £5 million, or uses up to 200,000 kWh a year of electricity. S4 (Energy Ombudsman) gives matching definitions, with small business expressed as fewer than 50 employees.
findings.limitations: S1 and S4 word the small-business employee threshold differently (11 to 50 versus fewer than 50). S1 is undated. S4 was last updated 24 March 2026. Large businesses get fewer protections, which these pages don't detail.

findings.claim: Ofgem announced (5 April 2024) that broker fees must be shown in contract principal terms for all non-domestic customers, and that suppliers may only use brokers that belong to a redress scheme for small business contracts. It also extended the Standards of Conduct to all businesses and required signposting to Citizens Advice.
findings.evidence: S3: from 1 July 2024 the Standards of Conduct apply to all businesses, and a new licence rule requires suppliers to signpost Micro Business consumers to Citizens Advice (and Citizens Advice Scotland). The signposting rule applies to Small Business consumers from December 2024, subject to the new definition entering legislation. The requirement to display broker fees in a contract's principal terms is extended from Micro Business consumers to all non-domestic customers, for contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024, and suppliers must make the information available on request. From December 2024, suppliers must only work with brokers (TPIs) that are members of a redress scheme when securing Small Business contracts. S3 names the Energy Ombudsman and the Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA) as schemes for broker disputes. S1 notes brokers are mostly paid commission by the supplier and that there is no cooling-off period after agreeing a contract.
findings.limitations: S3 is a press release from April 2024 announcing rules. Some changes are described as 'expected to be in place by the end of the year' or subject to legislation. I haven't verified final implementation from the licence conditions. The press release doesn't cover any commission-disclosure requirement before signing beyond the principal-terms rule.

findings.claim: Energy Ombudsman provides free dispute resolution for microbusinesses and small businesses against energy suppliers and brokers, after the firm's own complaints process has been used.
findings.evidence: S4: it offers free, independent dispute resolution to small businesses and microbusinesses, covering disputes with energy suppliers and energy brokers (and heat networks, network operators and others). The customer must first follow the supplier's or broker's complaints process. After 8 weeks, or once a deadlock letter or final response is issued, the Ombudsman may be able to help, subject to its Terms of Reference. S3 says the government's expanded Small Business definition lets businesses with fewer than 50 employees take complaints to the Energy Ombudsman. It also says Ofgem will update the Complaints Handling Standards so suppliers point Small Business consumers to the Ombudsman.
findings.limitations: Eligibility depends on meeting the Ombudsman's Terms of Reference, which I haven't read. Large businesses are not covered by the definitions cited. S4 was last updated 24 March 2026.

findings.claim: Switching rights depend on contract type. Fixed-term contracts usually carry exit fees and a switching window. Variable, evergreen, out-of-contract and deemed arrangements can be switched at any time.
findings.evidence: S2 (Ofgem): most suppliers won't let you switch before the end of a fixed contract unless a termination clause has been agreed or an exit fee is paid. A 'switching window' opens a few months before the contract ends, and you can sometimes switch in it without a fee. With variable-rate arrangements (rolling/evergreen, out-of-contract, deemed), you can switch at any time. A supplier may object to a switch, for example if you owe it money.
findings.limitations: The page has no date. Individual contract terms still need checking, and the page gives no fee amounts.

findings.claim: Ofgem describes a business energy price as covering wholesale energy cost, network costs and environmental (government decarbonisation scheme) costs. Wholesale is typically about 40% of an electricity bill, though the exact share varies.
findings.evidence: Ofgem blog (31 March 2026): the price "covers a range of costs including the wholesale energy cost (the cost to buy energy), network costs (the infrastructure to transport energy), and environmental costs (government decarbonisation schemes). Typically, wholesale costs can be about 40% of your electricity bill and about 60% of your gas bill, but exact percentages will vary."
findings.limitations: This is a blog post, not a full bill breakdown. It gives no percentages for network or policy costs and doesn't mention VAT. It doesn't say who sets each component in detail.

findings.claim: Recent and upcoming changes: network costs rose in April 2026 and wholesale prices are volatile. Contract lengths are returning to 3 to 5 years, and Ofgem advises care when recontracting.
findings.evidence: S5: "In April, network costs are increasing to upgrade energy infrastructure. Wholesale energy costs are volatile and will continue to be affected by the situation in the Middle East." Contract lengths are "starting to return to 3 to 5 years in length". Ofgem expects less than 10% of businesses to recontract in March and April, a further 10-12% to be on deemed contracts, and a further 10% to recontract in May to July. Suppliers may require security deposits, are not obliged to offer a contract, and there is no cooling-off period. Contract offers should be requested in writing if discussed by phone. It may be better to stay temporarily on deemed or out-of-contract rates if longer-term offers are high.
findings.limitations: It does not say whether network charge rises are passed through on fixed contracts. That depends on contract terms. The figures are Ofgem's expectations as of 31 March 2026.

findings.claim: Climate Change Levy (CCL) main rates for electricity are set out by HMRC: £0.00775 per kWh from 1 April 2025, rising to £0.00801 per kWh from 1 April 2026 and £0.00827 per kWh from 1 April 2027. Holders of a Climate Change Agreement (CCA) get a 92% discount on the electricity levy. Domestic consumers and charities (for non-business use) are not charged.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK (HMRC) main-rate table for electricity (£ per kWh): 0.00775 from 1 April 2025, 0.00801 from 1 April 2026, 0.00827 from 1 April 2027. The CCA percentage discount for electricity is 92% in every year shown. The rates "do not apply to taxable commodities supplied to domestic consumers and charities for non-business use". The business energy supplier is responsible for charging the correct levy. There are reduced rates for those in the climate change agreement scheme.
findings.limitations: The page was last updated 27 November 2025. It is rate guidance for suppliers and does not set out the eligibility criteria for CCA or other CCL exemptions (such as the de minimis, domestic-use or mineralogical/metallurgical exemptions). I did not read those.

findings.claim: Before signing, Ofgem says a business should know the contract type, term length, any fees (including those in special clauses), the protections it has, any broker fees or commission in the price, and what happens at the end of the contract (auto-renewal, or a move to out-of-contract or deemed rates).
findings.evidence: S1 (Ofgem) lists these points. It says contracts can be arranged directly or through a broker, consultant or price comparison service. Customers should check which suppliers a comparison site covers (whole market or a selection) and whether it receives commission. Brokers charge fees or are paid commission by the supplier, and brokers paid by a supplier must belong to an approved redress scheme. Customers should check this on the Energy Ombudsman broker register or the Utilities Intermediaries Association accredited list. There is no cooling-off period. S2 says to read the existing contract's terms for when you can switch, how much notice is needed and whether an exit fee applies. Switching needs your annual consumption and meter details, and a supplier may object to a switch, for example if you owe it money.
findings.limitations: Neither page is dated. Neither explains how to compare quotes like-for-like in detail, beyond checking term, fees, commission and the end-of-contract position.

findings.claim: Ofgem's March 2026 advice on recontracting: talk to your supplier about options and ask what contracts are available, short and long term. Be aware of security deposits, the lack of any obligation on suppliers to offer a contract, the lack of a cooling-off period, and the need for written terms. Submit regular meter readings or get a smart meter so you pay only for what you use.
findings.evidence: S5 (31 March 2026): "consider both short and long-term options. It may be better for you to temporarily stay on deemed or out of contract rates if the current longer-term contract offers are high." Suppliers may require security deposits. Energy suppliers "are not obliged to offer businesses a contract". You shouldn't feel pressured into signing, and if a contract is discussed by phone you should ask for it in writing before agreeing. Verify unexpected callers to avoid fraudsters. "To ensure you are only paying for what you use, submit regular meter readings or get a smart meter."
findings.limitations: This is a blog post, not formal guidance. It does not say how to check meter type, such as half-hourly versus non-half-hourly.

findings.claim: Efficiency advice and funding are signposted by Ofgem but not detailed. Ofgem points to the National Energy Foundation, the Energy Saving Trust, GOV.UK's Energy Technology List, the GOV.UK business finance and support finder, local councils, supplier schemes, the Smart Export Guarantee and Citizens Advice.
findings.evidence: S7: the National Energy Foundation offers free independent advice, and the Energy Saving Trust lists case studies and resources. The GOV.UK Energy Technology List covers independently verified energy-efficient products. Government schemes may offer loans, grants or subsidised measures, and supplier schemes vary by business size, location and sector. Citizens Advice offers free advice on business energy contracts and rights (0808 223 1133). Related content points to help if the business cannot afford its bills: call the supplier for a payment plan.
findings.limitations: The page is undated and partly outdated. It says the government is 'proposing' two new schemes from 2022 (Clean Heat Grant, Green Gas Support Scheme), so its scheme details should not be treated as current. It does not mention any successor to the Energy Bills Discount Scheme.

findings.claim: Ofgem administers the REGO scheme, which gives transparency on how much of a supplier's electricity comes from renewable sources. Ofgem's page lists REGO among the schemes it runs, and suppliers face obligations under many environmental schemes.
findings.evidence: S8 (Ofgem 'Environmental and social schemes') lists Renewable Energy Guarantees of Origin (REGO) among the schemes Ofgem administers on behalf of government. It says licensed electricity suppliers in Great Britain are obligated under many of these schemes, with the level depending on licence type, supply volumes and domestic customer count.
findings.limitations: The page's REGO section was collapsed, so I didn't read the REGO description. I therefore cannot state what a REGO certificate represents from this source, or how a business should verify a green tariff claim.

notes:
T1: I used the 2-search and 2-page limit, and read two Ofgem pages. Gaps: (1) I found no official source on how non-commodity charges (network, policy and levy costs) are passed through or fixed, or on whether 'fixed' contracts allow pass-through. (2) Nothing official on price-variation clauses. (3) No Citizens Advice or Energy Ombudsman business guidance was opened. (4) No typical termination-fee amounts or standing-charge figures. Further sources would be needed: Citizens Advice business energy pages, Energy Ombudsman, or Ofgem microbusiness licence conditions (SLC 7 and 7A).
T2: Searches surfaced an Ofgem page, 'Third Party Intermediaries: what your microbusiness needs to know'. I did not open it because of the page limit, and it would be a good source for microbusiness broker commission rules. I did not open the licence conditions (SLC 7A and others), so details of end-of-contract notice timing, such as how far in advance suppliers must send renewal notices, are not covered beyond the general statements in S1. Citizens Advice business guidance was also not opened.
T3: Gaps after using the page-open limit: (1) No official source read on VAT for business electricity (standard vs reduced rate, de minimis and charity supplies). (2) No official source on energy-intensive industry reliefs (British Industry Supercharger, EII exemption from policy costs, CCA eligibility criteria). (3) No Ofgem page on who sets each network and policy charge. (4) The only detail on the April 2026 network cost increases comes from the Ofgem blog, which gives no figures. S1 to S4 were read for earlier tasks and are not relevant to this one. Suggested follow-ups: Ofgem 'costs included in your bills' page, GOV.UK VAT on fuel and power guidance, and GOV.UK British Industry Supercharger guidance.
T4: Gaps: (1) The current status of the Energy Bills Discount Scheme and any successor, such as the British Industry Supercharger, was not covered. (2) No official source read on how to verify green tariff claims (REGO backing, Ofgem green tariff guidance). (3) No source on meter types (half-hourly versus non-half-hourly) or guidance on comparing quotes like-for-like beyond Ofgem's general points. (4) S7 is dated and out of step with current schemes. Suggested follow-ups: Ofgem's green energy tariff guidance, GOV.UK business energy support pages, Citizens Advice business energy pages, and the Energy Saving Trust or Carbon Trust.
